steps.body: Two box plots on the **same scale** answer two questions at a glance. Line up the median lines to compare **centres**; compare box widths to compare **spread**. Class A runs 8 to 18 with a box from 11 to 15. Class B runs 2 to 22 with a box from 9 to 17. Both medians sit at 13 — identical centres — but B's box is 8 wide against A's 4. Same typical value, very different consistency.
Put a number on the difference in consistency.

widget.prompt: Class A has Q1 = 11 and Q3 = 15. Class B has Q1 = 9 and Q3 = 17. How much wider is B's box than A's?

commonErrors.feedback: 8 is B's box width on its own (17 − 9). The question wants the difference between the widths: 8 − 4 = 4.
12 adds the two widths (8 + 4). To compare them, subtract: 8 − 4 = 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: A's box is 15 − 11 = 4 wide, B's is 17 − 9 = 8 wide, so B is 8 − 4 = 4 wider.

explanationVariants: Both medians are 13, so the typical score matches. B's box and whiskers stretch much further, so B's scores are far less consistent.
Centre and spread are separate questions. Here the centres tie and only the spread separates the classes — B is the more variable group.

widget.prompt: Class A and Class B both have a median of 13, but B's box and whiskers are much wider. What is the fair comparison?

options.label: Typical scores are the same; Class B's scores vary much more
options.feedback: Right — matching medians means matching centres, and the wider box and whiskers mean B is the less consistent class.

options.label: Class B did better overall because its plot reaches higher
options.feedback: B does reach 22, but it also drops to 2. A longer plot means more spread in both directions, not a higher typical score — the medians are tied at 13.

options.label: Class A has fewer students because its plot is shorter
options.feedback: Length shows the spread of values, never how many there are. A box plot of 10 scores and one of 200 scores can look identical.

explanationVariants: A's box spans 11 to 15 and B's spans 9 to 17, so every value in A's box range also lies inside B's — A's middle half sits entirely within B's.
B's box starts lower (9 < 11) and ends higher (17 > 15), so it completely contains A's box.

widget.prompt: A's box runs 11 to 15; B's box runs 9 to 17. How do the two middle halves relate?

options.label: A's middle half sits entirely inside the range of B's middle half
options.feedback: Yes — 9 < 11 and 17 > 15, so B's box swallows A's completely.

options.label: The two middle halves do not overlap at all
options.feedback: They overlap heavily — 11 to 15 is common to both boxes. Non-overlapping boxes would sit side by side with a gap.

options.label: They overlap only between 15 and 17
options.feedback: That is the part of B's box ABOVE A's. The shared stretch is all of 11 to 15, because A's box lies wholly within B's.

steps.body: One warning when comparing. A box plot hides the **individual values** — it shows only five numbers. Two very different data sets can produce the **same** box plot: one with values evenly sprinkled, one with values clumped at each end. If the question is about gaps, clusters or repeated values, go back to the dot plot; the box plot answers centre and spread.
Build the second plot so the medians match but the spreads do not.

widget.prompt: Draw Class B: min 2, Q1 9, median 13, Q3 17, max 22.
widget.successFeedback: That is Class B — same median line as A at 13, but a box twice as wide and whiskers reaching much further.
widget.orderFeedback: Keep the order min ≤ Q1 ≤ median ≤ Q3 ≤ max; one handle has passed its neighbour.
widget.valueFeedback: In order, but not yet on target. Check each handle against its number.

explanationVariants: Box plots report five summary numbers, so a gap in the middle of the data is invisible to them. A dot plot shows every value and would reveal the gap.
Only a display that draws individual values can show a hole in the data — the box plot would look completely normal.

widget.prompt: You suspect a data set has a gap — no values at all between 10 and 14. Which display would show it?

options.label: A dot plot, because it draws every individual value
options.feedback: Right — the empty stretch appears immediately as a hole in the dots. The box plot would hide it entirely.

options.label: A box plot, because the box would be split at the gap
options.feedback: A box plot is drawn from just five numbers and is never split. A gap inside the box leaves the picture looking completely ordinary.

options.label: Neither — a gap can never be seen in a display
options.feedback: A gap is very visible in the right display. A dot plot draws each value, so an empty stretch shows up as blank space.

explanationVariants: Bus median 24, walk median 12: the bus riders' typical trip is 24 − 12 = 12 minutes longer. Bus IQR = 30 − 18 = 12, walk IQR = 16 − 8 = 8, so the bus is also less predictable.
Compare the median lines for the centre gap (12 minutes) and the box widths for consistency (12 against 8, so the bus varies more).

widget.prompt: Bus trips: Q1 18, median 24, Q3 30. Walking trips: Q1 8, median 12, Q3 16. How many minutes longer is the bus riders' TYPICAL trip?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is the difference between the two IQRs (12 − 8), which compares consistency. The typical trip is the MEDIAN: 24 − 12 = 12.
36 adds the two medians (24 + 12). 'How much longer' asks for the difference: 24 − 12 = 12.
10 compares the Q1 values (18 − 8). The typical trip is measured at the median line, giving 24 − 12 = 12.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The typical value is the median. Bus 24, walking 12, so the bus trip is 24 − 12 = 12 minutes longer.

hints: 'Typical' points at one of the five numbers in particular.
Compare the two median lines, not the box edges.

takeaways: On a shared scale, median lines compare centres and box widths compare spread.
Equal medians with unequal boxes means the same typical value with different consistency.
Box plots hide individual values — use a dot plot when gaps or clusters matter.
steps.teaser: next: a spread measure built from the mean instead of the median — the typical distance from centre.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Comparing two box plots on one scale: **median lines** answer 'which centre is higher?' and **box widths** answer 'which group is more consistent?' A narrower box means a tighter, more predictable middle half.

explanationVariants: Team P's box is 30 − 26 = 4 wide; Team Q's is 34 − 22 = 12. The narrower box, P, is the more consistent team.
Consistency is about width, not position: 4 is narrower than 12, so Team P varies less.

widget.prompt: Team P's box runs 26 to 30. Team Q's box runs 22 to 34. Which team is more consistent?

options.label: Team P — its box is narrower
options.feedback: Right — a 4-wide box means P's middle half is packed tightly together.

options.label: Team Q — its box is wider
options.feedback: A wider box means MORE variation, not less. Q's middle half is spread over 12 units against P's 4.

options.label: They are equally consistent — the boxes overlap
options.feedback: Overlapping says the two groups cover common ground; consistency is about each box's own width, and 4 is much narrower than 12.
